# Introduction

This tutorial shows you how to create a [GitHub educational account](https://github.com/education), install [GitHub Desktop](https://github.com/apps/desktop) and download the course materials to your computer. It also covers the basics of Git and GitHub: committing changes, pushing them to GitHub and keeping your copy of the materials up to date. Finally, it shows you how to open the materials in [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/). I use GitHub Desktop here because it is the easiest option for beginners, but you are free to use any tool you like.

# What are Git and GitHub?

[Git](https://git-scm.com/) is a version control system. It keeps track of every change you make to your files, so you can go back to an older version or work on the same project with other people. [Linus Torvalds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linus_Torvalds), the creator of [Linux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linux), wrote Git in 2005, and it is now the [*de facto* standard for version control](https://stackoverflow.blog/2023/01/09/beyond-git-the-other-version-control-systems-developers-use/) in software development. Git is very powerful, but it can be hard to use at first. That is where GitHub comes in.

[GitHub](https://github.com) is a website that stores Git repositories online. You can keep all versions of your code in the cloud and work on it with other people. GitHub also has tools for reporting bugs and managing projects, and it can even [host your website for free](https://pages.github.com/) (this course website is hosted there!). Most open-source projects live on GitHub, and many companies use it too, such as [Microsoft](https://github.com/microsoft), [Google](https://github.com/google) and [Meta](https://github.com/facebook)[^apollo]. You can think of GitHub as a social network for programmers, where you can follow other people, star their projects and contribute to them.

[^apollo]: As a curiosity, the code for the [Apollo 11 mission](https://github.com/chrislgarry/Apollo-11) is also on GitHub.

We will use GitHub throughout the course, so it is a good idea to get familiar with it now. GitHub is free, including private repositories. Here is how to get started:

1. **Create a GitHub account.** Go to <https://github.com/> and click on "Sign up" (top right). Use your Emory email address, as you will need it for the educational account below. Please choose your username carefully, because everyone will be able to see it

![GitHub sign-up page](images/github-signup.png)

2. **Apply to GitHub Education.** Go to <https://github.com/education>, click on "Join GitHub Education" and follow the instructions. You will need to show that you are a student, for example with your student ID card. Once GitHub approves your application, you will get the GitHub Student Developer Pack, which includes free access to [Copilot Student](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/about-github-copilot/plans-for-github-copilot) and many other tools

![GitHub Education](images/github-education.png)

3. **Download and install GitHub Desktop.** You can download it from <https://desktop.github.com/>. GitHub Desktop lets you use Git with buttons and menus instead of typing commands in the terminal. It is available for Windows and macOS

![GitHub Desktop](images/github-desktop.png)

After you install GitHub Desktop, sign in with your GitHub account. You should then see this screen:

![GitHub Desktop after signing in](images/github-desktop-signin.png)

You are now ready to use Git and GitHub. Let us download the course materials.

# Downloading the course materials

The course materials are on GitHub at <https://github.com/danilofreire/datasci151-summer>. First, you will "fork" the repository, which creates your own copy of it in your GitHub account. Go to the repository page, click on "Fork" in the top-right corner and then on "Create a new fork".

![Forking the repository](images/github-fork.png)

![Creating your copy of the repository](images/github-fork02.png)

GitHub will ask you to name your copy. I recommend that you keep the same name I use (`datasci151-summer`), as this makes it easier to follow the instructions in class. Then click on "Create fork".

*You only need to do this once.* Your fork stays connected to my repository, so you can download my updates whenever I add new materials.

Next, you will "clone" your fork, which downloads a copy of it to your computer. On your fork's page, click on the green "Code" button and copy the URL. Please make sure you copy the URL of *your fork*, not of my repository: the URL should contain your username.

Open GitHub Desktop and click on "Clone a Repository from the Internet". Paste the URL, choose the folder where you want to save the materials and click on "Clone".

![Click on "Clone a Repository from the Internet"](images/github-clone01.png)

![Click on "URL", paste the repository URL and click on "Clone"](images/github-clone02.png)

![Cloning the repository](images/github-clone03.png)

GitHub Desktop will then ask how you plan to use the fork. Select "To contribute to the parent project" and click on "Continue". This option lets you download my updates later. The other option creates a copy with no link to my repository, so you would not see any changes I make. If you choose it by mistake, you can fix it this way:

- Remove the repository from GitHub Desktop (right-click on the repository name and select "Remove")
- Delete the folder from your computer
- Clone your fork again, as explained above

![Choosing how to use the fork](images/github-clone04.png)

*And you are done!* You now have the course materials on your computer. To open them in VS Code, click on "Repository" > "Open in Visual Studio Code" in GitHub Desktop.

![Opening the repository in VS Code](images/github-open-vscode.png)

# Saving your changes

Now that you have the course materials on your computer, let us see the three steps you will use most often: change, commit and push.

1. *Change your files.* GitHub Desktop shows every change you make to your files in the "Changes" tab. In the image below, you can see that I have changed a few files

![The "Changes" tab](images/github-desktop-changes.png)

The "History" tab shows all the commits in the repository. Green lines are text you added, and red lines are text you removed.

![The "History" tab](images/github-desktop-history.png)

2. *Commit your changes.* A commit is a snapshot of your files that you can go back to later. To commit, write a short description of your changes in the "Summary" box and click on "Commit to main"[^main]. A clear summary, such as "Finish exercise 2 of lecture 05", makes it much easier to find a change later

[^main]: `main` is the name of the default branch in GitHub. You will make all your changes there in this course. Programmers also create other branches to work on new features or bug fixes without changing `main`.

![Committing changes](images/github-desktop-commit.png)

Your commit will then appear in the "History" tab:

![The commit in the "History" tab](images/github-desktop-commit02.png)

3. *Push your changes to GitHub.* Commits are saved only on your computer until you push them. To send them to your fork on GitHub, click on "Repository" > "Push"

![Push and fetch](images/github-desktop-push.png)

You will also see a "Fetch" option. "Push" uploads your commits to GitHub, and "Fetch" checks GitHub for changes you do not have yet. We will use it in the next section.

# Updating the course materials

I will update the course materials often, with new lectures, fixes and improvements. To get these updates, you need to download them from my repository. Before you start, please commit all your changes, as explained in the previous section.

1. In GitHub Desktop, click on the "Branch" menu and select "Update from upstream/main"
   - "upstream" is my original repository
   - "main" is the main branch of the repository

![Updating from upstream](images/github-desktop-update.png)

Some practical advice:

- Please update your materials *at the start of every class*, so you always have the latest version
- If you want to change one of my files, save your version *with a different file name*. Otherwise, my updates may overwrite your changes
- Your fork is public, and GitHub does not let you make a fork of a public repository private. So please do not save anything in your fork that you do not want others to see, such as your answers to the assignments

And that is it! You now know how to use Git and GitHub to manage your code. If you have any questions, just send me an email and I will be happy to help. Good luck!

# Further resources

- [GitHub Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started): GitHub's official guides for beginners
- [GitHub Skills](https://skills.github.com/): short, hands-on courses to practise Git and GitHub
- [GitHub Desktop documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/desktop): everything about GitHub Desktop
- [Pro Git](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2): a free book that covers Git in detail
- [Software Carpentry: Version Control with Git](https://swcarpentry.github.io/git-novice/): a free lesson for beginners
- [How to use Git and GitHub Desktop (YouTube)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MaqVvXv6zrU): a video that covers the basics of GitHub Desktop
